## torment

tormented; tormenting; torments

tor·​ment, TOR-ment,  *transitive verb*

: to cause severe, usually persistent or recurrent distress of the body or mind

Examples:

“The cattle were tormented by flies.”

“He was tormented by doubt.”

“She liked me, but she laughed at me, and tormented me…” — Charles Dickens

In this work, torment names the sustained, deliberate infliction of such distress — the felt experience produced by Zersetzung tactics and by what is here called psychological smothering: the cumulative, suffocating pressure of relentless, inescapable harassment meant to wear a person down.

Neuroscience: Persistent torment is a form of chronic psychological stress, which has measurable effects on the brain and body. Prolonged stress keeps the HPA axis and the stress hormone cortisol elevated, and is associated with structural and functional changes in the hippocampus (memory), amygdala (fear and threat response), and prefrontal cortex (regulation and judgment) — a cumulative physiological toll often described as allostatic load.

Related terms: [Zersetzung tactics](/glossary/zersetzung-tactics), [psychological smothering](/glossary/psychological-smothering), [No-touch torture](/glossary/no-touch-torture), [chilling effect](/glossary/chilling-effect), [Gaslighting](/glossary/gaslighting)

Sources: [Merriam-Webster](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/torment); [Chronic stress and the hippocampus — Frontiers in Synaptic Neuroscience](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/synaptic-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnsyn.2010.00024/full)

## terrorism

ter·ror·ism,   TAIR-uh-riz-uhm,   *noun*

: the systematic use of terror, especially as a means of coercion. — Merriam-Webster

: violent, criminal acts committed by individuals and/or groups to further ideological goals stemming from domestic influences — political, religious, social, racial, or environmental in nature. — FBI (domestic terrorism)

: violent, criminal acts committed by individuals and/or groups who are inspired by, or associated with, designated foreign terrorist organizations or nations (state-sponsored). — FBI (international terrorism)

Examples:

“the fight against terrorism”

“The British Columbia prosecution service said that Lo could face more charges, but investigators ruled out terrorism and said Lo had a history of mental health issues.” —Mark Weinstein, MSNBC Newsweek, 28 Apr. 2025

“If a cyberattack is to blame for the loss of power, Judge Jorge Calama would then investigate the case as a potential act of terrorism, according to court documents.” —Julia Gomez, USA Today, 29 Apr. 2025

Related terms: [Zersetzung tactics](/glossary/zersetzung-tactics), [No-touch torture](/glossary/no-touch-torture), [Directed-energy](/glossary/directed-energy)

Sources: [Merriam-Webster](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/terrorism); [FBI — Terrorism](https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/terrorism)

## brain-data-as-a-service ([brain.space](http://brain.space))

: The first end-to-end EEG system from [brain.space](http://brain.space) that extracts, labels and analyzes data in real time. The perfect solution for the researcher EEG needs. Proprietary hardware: automated process non-invasively and accurately collects brain data with the click of a button. Brain Data is de-noised, standardized and automatically tagged by ML models. Analytic tools provide two levels of Brain Data analysis: clean data for research and Brain Insights.

*—*[*Brain.Space*](http://brain.space)

Related terms: [software-as-a-service](/glossary/software-as-a-service-saas), [brain–computer interface](/glossary/braincomputer-interface-bci), [electroencephalogram](/glossary/electroencephalogram), [artificial intelligence](/glossary/artificial-intelligence), [hardware](/glossary/hardware-computer)

## euthanasia

eu·​tha·​na·​sia, yoo-thuh-NAY-zhee-uh,  *noun*

: the act or practice of killing or permitting the death of hopelessly sick or injured individuals (such as persons or domestic animals) in a relatively painless way for reasons of mercy

Examples:

“While most states have felony-level cruelty laws, many exempt activities like research, euthanasia, farming, hunting, pest control, and rodeos.” —Lucy Notarantonio, MSNBC Newsweek, 12 July 2025

“Already euthanasia has become the 5th leading cause of death north of our border.” —Krista Kafer, Denver Post, 7 July 2025

Sources: [Merriam-Webster](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/euthanasia)

## hardware

hard·​ware,    HARD-wair,   *noun*

: the physical components — such as electronic and electrical devices — of a computer or other apparatus

Example:

“But more recently, some companies have been working toward mating AI technology with hardware.” —Alan Stafford, Forbes.com, 1 May 2025

In neuroscience and neuro-technology, hardware refers to the physical devices that record from or stimulate the nervous system. It ranges from non-invasive equipment worn on or near the body — EEG electrode caps and headsets, MEG and fMRI scanners, fNIRS sensors, and stimulation devices such as TMS coils or tDCS pads — to partially and fully invasive implants placed on or within brain tissue, including electrocorticography (ECoG) grids, depth electrodes, and microelectrode arrays such as the Utah array. This hardware is typically paired with amplifiers, signal-processing units, and software that turn raw neural activity into data or commands.

Related terms: [software](/glossary/software), [brain–computer interface](/glossary/braincomputer-interface-bci), [electroencephalograph](/glossary/electroencephalogram), [transparent brain-computer interfaces](/glossary/transparent-brain-computer-interfaces-bcis)

## artificial intelligence

ar·ti·fi·cial in·tel·li·gence,   ar-duh-fish-uhl uhn-TEL-uh-juhns,   *noun*

: the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior

: the theory and development of computer systems able to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as visual perception, speech recognition, decision-making, and translation between languages

Examples:

“A Monmouth University poll … found that only 9 percent of Americans believed that computers with artificial intelligence would do more good than harm to society.” —Shira Ovide

Related terms: [software](/glossary/software), [brain-data-as-a-service](/glossary/brain-data-as-a-service-brain-spacehttp-brain-space), [cognitive liberty](/glossary/cognitive-liberty)

## perceptual set

per·SEP·choo·uhl set,   *noun*

A perceptual set is a tendency to perceive or notice some aspects of the available sensory data and ignore others. It is heavily influenced by expectations, past experience, and context. If an object is completely outside a person's prior experience (their “set”), they may not select it for conscious attention — effectively rendering it “invisible” to the mind's eye, even if the retinas physically register it.

This principle gives the archive its name. In an often-told story — variously attributed to the arrival of Magellan's ships off Tierra del Fuego and to Captain Cook's Endeavour off the Australian coast — the people onshore are said to have been unable to see the European vessels at first, because nothing in their prior experience had prepared them to perceive such a thing, until someone learned to recognize the strange disturbance on the water and taught others where to look. The anecdote is almost certainly apocryphal, but the principle it dramatizes is real and measurable.

## software

soft·​ware,   SAWFFT-wair,   *noun*

: the instructions that control what a computer does; computer programs

Example:

“He's written a piece of software that does your taxes for you.”

In neuroscience and neuro-technology, software refers to the programs and algorithms that turn raw neural activity into usable information — filtering and de-noising signals, decoding brain data into commands, and increasingly using machine-learning models to label, interpret, or reconstruct patterns of thought. It is the counterpart to neuro-technology hardware: the hardware records from or stimulates the nervous system, while the software makes sense of what is recorded and directs what is sent.

Related terms: [hardware](/glossary/hardware-computer), [software-as-a-service](/glossary/software-as-a-service-saas), [artificial intelligence](/glossary/artificial-intelligence), [brain-data-as-a-service](/glossary/brain-data-as-a-service-brain-spacehttp-brain-space)

## Electroencephalography (EEG)

elec·tro·en·ceph·a·log·ra·phy,   uh-leck-troh-en-seff-uh-LOG-ruh-fee,   *noun*

: the recording of the brain’s electrical activity, usually measured non-invasively through electrodes placed on the scalp.

The apparatus that detects and records this activity is an **electroencephalograph**, and the tracing it produces is an **electroencephalogram** — both abbreviated EEG. Electroencephalography is widely used in medicine and neuroscience, and is a common signal source for brain–computer interfaces.

Example:

“Perri’s setup begins with a headset that measures the electrical activity in her brain, known as an electroencephalogram (EEG for short).” —Christopher Cruz, Rolling Stone, 10 July 2024

Related terms: [brain–computer interface](/glossary/braincomputer-interface-bci), [hardware](/glossary/hardware-computer)

## telepathy

te·​lep·​a·​thy,   tuh-LEP-uh-thee,   *noun*

adjective form: telepathic (tel-uh-PATH-ik)

: communication from one mind to another by extrasensory means

Examples:

“The next year, Schmeisser marched into a large conference room at Army Research Office headquarters in Research Triangle Park, North Carolina, to pitch a research project to investigate synthetic telepathy for soldiers.” —Adam Piore, Discover Magazine, 1 Mar. 2012

“You need to tell me what you're thinking. I'm not telepathic.” (adjective form)

In neuroscience, what was once framed as purely extrasensory is now pursued through brain–computer interfaces that decode neural activity into communication or device control. Neuralink named its first product “Telepathy,” a brain implant intended to let a person operate a computer or phone by thought alone, and its VOICE study is an early-feasibility trial of an implanted BCI for “communication restoration.” In 2026, VOICE participant Kenneth Shock — an ALS patient who had lost the ability to speak — used the N1 implant to communicate through thought alone, his intended words voiced by a synthesized recreation of his own pre-ALS voice; Neuralink published video of the demonstration. Such work reframes telepathy as an emerging technological capability: communication that bypasses the body by reading from, and writing to, the brain.

Related terms: [brain–computer interface](/glossary/braincomputer-interface-bci), [cursor control](/glossary/cursor-control-bci), [Voice-to-skull](/glossary/voice-to-skull), [cognitive liberty](/glossary/cognitive-liberty), [Diving](/glossary/diving)

Sources: [Neuralink trademark filing — MobiHealthNews](https://www.mobihealthnews.com/news/elon-musks-neuralink-files-trademark-blindsight-telepathy-and-telekinesis); [VOICE study — ClinicalTrials.gov](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07224256); [Translating Thought to Speech — Neuralink](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u8mmn9lOIyw)

## software-as-a-service (SaaS)

: A cloud-based software delivery model in which users access applications over the internet — typically through a web browser — instead of installing and managing them locally. The provider handles the underlying infrastructure, security, maintenance, and updates, and access is sold on a subscription basis. The “as-a-service” model has since been extended to other domains, including brain data — see brain-data-as-a-service.

Related terms: [brain-data-as-a-service](/glossary/brain-data-as-a-service-brain-spacehttp-brain-space), [software](/glossary/software)

## brain–computer interface (BCI)

: A brain–computer interface (BCI), sometimes called a brain–machine interface (BMI), is a direct communication link between the brain's electrical activity and an external device, most commonly a computer or robotic limb. BCIs are often directed at researching, mapping, assisting, augmenting, or repairing human cognitive or sensory-motor functions. They are often conceptualized as a human–machine interface that skips the intermediary of moving body parts (e.g. hands or feet). BCI implementations range from non-invasive (EEG, MEG, MRI) and partially invasive (ECoG and endovascular) to invasive (microelectrode array), based on how physically close electrodes are to brain tissue.

*—*[*Wikipedia*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain%E2%80%93computer_interface)

Related terms: [cursor control](/glossary/cursor-control-bci), [transparent brain-computer interfaces](/glossary/transparent-brain-computer-interfaces-bcis), [electroencephalogram](/glossary/electroencephalogram), [hardware](/glossary/hardware-computer), [software](/glossary/software), [telepathy](/glossary/telepathy), [cognitive liberty](/glossary/cognitive-liberty)

## cognitive liberty

An evolving concept asserting the fundamental right of an individual to sovereignty over their own mind and consciousness. It extends the traditional right to “freedom of thought” to address challenges raised by neuroscience and technology — brain–computer interfaces that can read from or write to the brain, neuro-enhancements that alter memory or attention, and AI systems that can exploit cognitive biases, micro-target persuasion, or reconstruct thoughts from brain data. These developments raise pressing ethical and legal questions about mental privacy and manipulation. At its core, cognitive liberty protects the individual's control over their most private sphere — the mind — and is often described as a prerequisite for all other freedoms, since the ability to think freely underlies freedom of speech, belief, and action.

Related terms: [brain–computer interface](/glossary/braincomputer-interface-bci), [artificial intelligence](/glossary/artificial-intelligence), [telepathy](/glossary/telepathy), [chilling effect](/glossary/chilling-effect)

## transparent brain-computer interfaces (BCIs)

: Brain–computer interfaces built from optically transparent electrode materials — typically graphene, a nanomaterial — so that electrical activity can be recorded at the same time the underlying brain tissue is observed through the device using optical imaging (such as two-photon microscopy). Because the array is see-through, researchers can pair surface electrical recordings with a direct optical view of deeper neural activity, and AI (machine-learning models) can learn the correlation between the two — predicting deep-brain activity from surface signals alone. The approach allows longer observation of a freely moving subject and may make future implants less invasive.

Related terms: [brain–computer interface](/glossary/braincomputer-interface-bci), [hardware](/glossary/hardware-computer), [artificial intelligence](/glossary/artificial-intelligence)

Sources: [Cami Rosso, “Transparent Brain-Computer Interface Uses AI and Nanotech,” Psychology Today, Jan 24 2024](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-future-brain/202401/transparent-brain-computer-interface-uses-ai-and-nanotech); [Underlying study — Nature Nanotechnology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-023-01576-z)

## cursor control (BCI)

The use of a brain–computer interface to move and click an on-screen cursor through neural signals alone, without physical movement of the hand. It is one of the most established demonstrations of BCI technology, used chiefly as an assistive tool for people with paralysis or severe motor impairment.

Example:

“Mind-Controlled Cursor Could Allow Disabled to Type and Click With Ease. A new way of allowing paralyzed or severely injured people to control on-screen cursors taps directly into the brain and shows great promise.” —NBC News, July 2015

Related terms: [brain–computer interface](/glossary/braincomputer-interface-bci), [telepathy](/glossary/telepathy)

## chilling effect

When individuals or groups are discouraged from exercising their legal or natural rights — such as freedom of speech — out of fear of legal, social, or economic consequences. It can be produced by laws, regulations, or private actions that are overly broad, vague, or inconsistently applied, leading people to self-censor to avoid punishment or retaliation. In U.S. First Amendment terms it is a significant concern: by stifling open discourse on controversial or unpopular topics, it makes it harder for the public to hold officials and powerful institutions accountable.

Related terms: [cognitive liberty](/glossary/cognitive-liberty), [torment](/glossary/torment), [psychological smothering](/glossary/psychological-smothering)
